narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 70% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first try. That does not mean failure is certain; it means your profile resembled applicants who more often did not pass, and the admissions decision treated that risk as too high.

The strongest factor was your LSAT score. At 32, it was below the average of 37.18 among accepted students, and it was the main reason the model leaned toward bar-exam failure. The second most important factor was your third-year class standing decile. Your decile of 8 actually pushed the prediction toward passing, so it worked in your favor and was not the reason for denial. The third factor was your family income bracket. Being from a middle-income family pushed slightly toward failure, though much less strongly than your LSAT score; this is background information rather than something you can change.

To improve a future application, focus on the factor you can most directly address: strengthen your LSAT preparation and consider retaking the exam if feasible. Ask the admissions office whether you can discuss your profile, submit an appeal, or receive guidance for reapplication. You may also provide context for your third-year standing and any bar-readiness steps you plan to take. Because gender and race were not used, your denial was not based on those characteristics.
